texto:
Brand equity is the value a name adds to a product over and above what the product does. Two identical bottles of cola, one carrying a famous label and one carrying none, sell at different prices and in different volumes. The gap between them, in price and in how often buyers choose it, is brand equity. The concept exists because a large share of what companies spend on advertising produces no immediate sale, and finance departments, acquirers and marketers needed a way to describe what that spending leaves behind.
The term carries two meanings that are often blurred: the psychological stock of associations held in buyers' memories, and the cash value of that stock to the company that owns the name. Academic models describe the first; rankings and valuation standards price the second.
How brand equity works
Kevin Lane Keller gave the field its most cited definition in the January 1993 issue of the Journal of Marketing. He described customer-based brand equity as "the differential effect that knowledge about the brand has on consumer response to marketing activity for the brand." Equity is positive when people respond more favourably to an advertisement, a price rise or a new product because they know the name, and negative when the name makes them respond worse than they would to an unbranded version. Keller split brand knowledge into two parts: awareness, whether the name is recognised and recalled, and image, the associations attached to it.
David Aaker, a professor at the University of California, Berkeley, had published Managing Brand Equity two years earlier, in 1991. His model treats equity as a set of assets and liabilities linked to a brand's name and symbol that add to or subtract from the value a product provides. It groups them into five categories: brand loyalty, name awareness, perceived quality, brand associations and other proprietary assets such as trademarks, patents and channel relationships.
Keller later turned his definition into a ladder. In a 2001 Marketing Science Institute working paper, report 01-107, he set out the customer-based brand equity pyramid, which runs from salience at the base, through performance and imagery, to judgements and feelings, and finally to resonance, the level at which buyers are loyal and actively engaged. The bottom layer, salience, now has its own measurement literature.
In practice, equity is tracked through surveys of awareness, consideration, preference and attribute associations, and inferred from behaviour such as price premiums over private label, repeat purchase rates and branded search volume. Campaign-level surveys, such as brand lift studies, measure short-term movements in some of the same attitudes, while mix models estimate how much of a brand's baseline sales those attitudes support.
From memory to money
Turning equity into a dollar figure is a separate discipline, brand valuation. Three firms publish annual league tables, each with a different method.
Interbrand starts with economic profit: a brand's forecast after-tax operating profit, minus a capital charge for the factories, distribution and working capital that produced it. It then applies a Role of Brand Index, the share of purchase decisions attributed to the brand rather than price or features. The resulting brand earnings are discounted at a rate derived from a 0 to 100 Brand Strength score, built from ten factors: four internal (direction, alignment, empathy, agility) and six external (distinctiveness, coherence, participation, presence, trust, affinity).
Kantar's BrandZ takes the parent company's earnings, applies an intangible ratio and an attribution rate to isolate branded earnings, and multiplies the result by a brand multiple. That "financial value" is then scaled by brand contribution, the share driven by brand equity alone, measured through consumer surveys on whether a brand is meaningful, different and salient. According to Kantar, the survey base covers more than 4.6 million interviews across 54 markets and 22,392 brands.
Brand Finance uses royalty relief, which asks what a company would pay to license its own name if it did not own it. Forecast revenues are multiplied by a sector royalty rate, adjusted by a Brand Strength Index.
Two International Organization for Standardization (ISO) documents govern the field. ISO 10668, published in 2010, sets requirements for monetary brand valuation. ISO 20671, published in 2019 and renumbered ISO 20671-1 in November 2021, covers non-financial brand evaluation, the measurement of the inputs and outputs that drive value.
Origins and evolution
The phrase came into wide use in the late 1980s, when a wave of takeovers put prices on brands that balance sheets ignored. In 1988 Rank Hovis McDougall, the British food group, faced a hostile bid from Goodman Fielder Wattie. It hired Interbrand to value its brand portfolio, argued that the offer undervalued the company, and saw the bid rebuffed, according to a 2019 retrospective by Interbrand executives. The same year the Marketing Science Institute published a conference summary, report 88-104, titled "Defining, measuring, and managing brand equity".
Keller's 1993 paper named the two motives explicitly: a "financially based motivation to estimate the value of a brand more precisely" for accounting and deals, and a "strategy-based motivation to improve marketing productivity". Interbrand launched its global ranking around 2000 and Kantar's BrandZ ranking followed in 2006. The ISO standards arrived in 2010 and 2019.
Accounting rules have not moved as far. Under International Accounting Standard (IAS) 38, internally generated brands cannot be recognised as assets. A brand bought separately or acquired with a business appears on the balance sheet, and one with an indefinite life is tested annually for impairment rather than amortised. A company that builds a famous name from nothing therefore reports no asset for it under International Financial Reporting Standards, while a rival that buys an equivalent brand does.
Why it matters for marketers
Brand equity is the stock that brand advertising is supposed to build, and many measurement disputes concern how to see it. Google's Effectiveness Equation report found that marketing returns in months 5 to 24 equal those of the first four months, the gap captured by the long-term ROI multiplier. TransUnion and MMA Global case studies reported long-term lift up to six times the short-term effect. YouTube's creator marketing materials cited a Google-commissioned Circana analysis that modelled long-term returns through brand equity pathways.
Equity also shows up in price. Strong brands can hold prices without losing volume, which is the subject of pricing power. Kantar and IPA research presented in October 2026 found that 75% of UK consumer goods leaders could not say whether their price promotions paid, and described brands that promote repeatedly as 1.2 times more price elastic. Les Binet, the effectiveness researcher, likened them to class A drugs: "expensive, dangerous and addictive."
Limitations and disputes
The valuations disagree by multiples. For the same brand in roughly the same period, Interbrand put Apple at $470.9 billion in October 2025, Brand Finance put it at $607.6 billion in January 2026, and Kantar BrandZ put it at $1.38 trillion in 2026. Interbrand's top 100 totalled $3.6 trillion; Kantar's top 100 totalled $13.1 trillion. None can be checked against a market price, because brands are rarely sold apart from the businesses that use them.
The academic models face a different challenge. Researchers at the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute, led by Byron Sharp and Jenni Romaniuk, argue that most of what tracking surveys call loyalty or differentiation is a by-product of size: big brands have more buyers, who are slightly more loyal and more likely to recall them. Sharp, Romaniuk and Andrew Ehrenberg reported in 2007 that across 17 markets only about 11% of a brand's users described it as different. On that view, attitudes follow purchase more than they cause it, and equity metrics risk measuring market share twice.
Measurement windows add a third problem. Equity effects build over years, but most campaign evaluation runs over weeks.
Not the same as
- Brand value is the monetary output of a valuation, a dollar figure. Brand equity is the underlying set of memories and behaviours that produce it.
- Brand awareness and salience are components of equity, not equity itself.
- Brand lift is a survey measure of how one campaign shifted attitudes such as ad recall or consideration, over weeks. It captures a change in a slice of equity, not the stock.
- Goodwill is an accounting entry for the premium paid in an acquisition over identifiable net assets. Acquired brands are recognised separately from goodwill under IAS 38. Brand verification, a platform check of trademark ownership, is unrelated despite the shared word.
Recent developments
Kantar's 2026 BrandZ ranking, the 21st edition, put Google at number one for the first time since 2018, with a value of $1.48 trillion, up 57%. AI products entered the table: Claude debuted at number 27 at $96.6 billion, and ChatGPT recorded the ranking's largest year-on-year increase, 285%. Interbrand's 2026 edition had not been published as of October 13, 2026.
AI shopping tools are changing where equity is tested. Kantar's trends report warned that salience alone will not make brands algorithmically preferred and that brands not chosen as an AI agent's default recommendation risk being "optimized out." An instruction file attributed to Meta's Muse shopping agent, reported on October 12, 2026, called ranking well-known merchants among the top five picks "imperative". Google, for its part, claimed in June 2026 that each additional branded search after an ad view is worth an average $31 increase in sales, without disclosing a method.
Private label reached 38.5% of European grocery value in 2024, and an Adtaxi survey found 40% of Americans had switched to lower-cost brands. In January 2026, an IPA paper by Charlie Ebdy of Omnicom Media Group UK prompted a public exchange over whether advertising can still build brands at past rates.
Timeline
- 1988: Rank Hovis McDougall commissions Interbrand to value its brands while fighting a hostile bid from Goodman Fielder Wattie
- 1988: Marketing Science Institute publishes report 88-104, "Defining, measuring, and managing brand equity"
- 1989: London Stock Exchange endorses brand valuation, according to Interbrand
- 1991: David Aaker publishes Managing Brand Equity, setting out five asset categories
- January 1993: Kevin Lane Keller defines customer-based brand equity in the Journal of Marketing
- 2001: Keller publishes the brand equity pyramid in Marketing Science Institute report 01-107
- 2006: Kantar BrandZ global ranking first published
- 2010: ISO 10668 on monetary brand valuation published
- 2019: ISO 20671 on brand evaluation published
- November 2021: ISO 20671 renumbered as ISO 20671-1
- October 15, 2025: Interbrand Best Global Brands 2025 values the top 100 at $3.6 trillion, Apple first at $470.9 billion
- January 23, 2026: Brand Finance Global 500 2026 values Apple at $607.6 billion
- April 14, 2026: Kantar applies its latest BrandZ methodology changes
- 2026: Kantar BrandZ ranks Google first at $1.48 trillion; total top 100 value reaches $13.1 trillion
- October 7, 2026: Kantar and IPA present research on price promotions at the IPA Effectiveness Conference

Summary
Who: Academics David Aaker and Kevin Lane Keller defined the concept; Interbrand, Kantar and Brand Finance put dollar values on it; ISO sets valuation and evaluation standards; marketers, finance teams and acquirers use it.
What: The value a brand name adds to a product beyond its function, held in buyers' awareness and associations and expressed in price premiums, loyalty and cash flows.
When: Popularised in the late 1980s takeover wave, defined academically in 1991 and 1993, standardised in 2010 and 2019, and ranked annually since around 2000.
Where: In consumers' memories, in tracking surveys and mix models, in acquisition accounting under IAS 38, and in annual brand rankings.
Why: It describes what brand advertising leaves behind when no sale follows immediately, and it gives companies a basis for pricing, budgeting and valuing businesses.
